title: lex-os trust manifest
description: The owner's complete safety declaration. Once an agent is dispatched no human watches, so this document IS the safety boundary — everything the runtime enforces is derived from it. Written by whoever holds the authority being granted; read by the Lex type checker, the supervisor, and every downstream gate. Worked examples: demo/*.json, starting with demo/manifest.json.

egress.description: The only hosts the box may reach, as `host` or `host:port`. A leading `*.` matches subdomains. An EMPTY list grants no egress — it does not mean unrestricted. Both the static type check and the kernel firewall are derived from this list, so it is the allowlist in the literal sense.

actuation.description: The robot half of the grant. Omit or null for an ordinary agent box; when present the supervisor mediates every skill's arguments against it.

facets.description: Authority domains lex-os does not itself model, keyed by facet name — `infra` for a Terraform plan, `pod` for an admission wall. Deliberately type-erased here: the consuming gate supplies a registry that narrows them. An UNREGISTERED facet must be byte-identical between parent and child, which is safe rather than permissive.

_comment.description: Free-text notes; the one reserved key, because JSON has no comment syntax and these manifests carry real reasoning. Ignored by every decision and excluded from the content address, so annotating a manifest never re-identifies it. Note it is exactly `_comment`, not a prefix: `_comment_foo` is refused like any other unknown field.

Goal.description: What the agent is asked to accomplish. An object, not a string.

done_signal.description: A token the agent reports to claim completion. The supervisor treats reaching it as ONE terminal condition, never the only one — budget exhaustion and kill always win.

Grant.description: The capability grant: the same declaration the Lex type checker uses to reject a program calling an un-granted effect, and the one the supervisor turns into an OS sandbox policy. One declaration, two enforcement layers.

Level.description: One authority level. NOTE: all three axes share this single enum, so a level whose name belongs to another axis is accepted today even though it means nothing there — `exec: "Allowlist"` parses and outranks `Sandboxed`. That is a known defect (alpibrusl/lex-lang#808), not a feature to use. Per axis, the levels that are meaningful are: filesystem — None, ReadOnly, ReadWrite, Full; network — None, Loopback, Allowlist, Full; exec — None, Sandboxed, Full. Ordering is by rank: None=0; ReadOnly, Sandboxed, Loopback=1; ReadWrite, Allowlist=2; Full=3. A child manifest may only narrow, and narrowing compares rank.

Budget.description: Hard, externally-enforced bounds. External because a stuck or misaligned agent will not honour its own limits; on exhaustion the box halts regardless of goal state. These four fields are the whole budget — there is no CPU or memory ceiling here, and inventing one is refused rather than ignored.

wall_clock_secs.description: Wall-clock ceiling in seconds. Job-shaped: a long-running service has no natural value here (lex-os#89).

max_commands.description: Maximum MEDIATED commands the agent may issue — supervisor-mediated effects, not inbound requests.

max_money_cents.description: Maximum spend, in integer cents. Never a float: budgets must be exact. Consumers read this differently — forecast spend for a Terraform plan, committed reservation for a Kubernetes namespace.

max_api_calls.description: Maximum external API calls — a sub-budget of network egress, so outbound only.

IsolationFloor.description: The MINIMUM isolation strength the owner requires. The resolver maps this plus the grant to a backend and REFUSES rather than downgrades if the environment cannot reach the floor. A grant also implies a floor on its own: exec None implies Namespace, exec Full implies MicroVm, anything between implies Gvisor — the owner may raise it, never lower it.
